en: The *Sūtra on the Skillful Means of Adorning with Joyful Necklaces*, also titled the *Sūtra of the Questions and Answers of the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kasmīra during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus;
and eight thousand bodhisattvas, all well-known to the world, who had attained the various supernatural powers and dhāraṇīs,
possessed unimpeded eloquence, were fully accomplished in the patience of the non-arising of phenomena, and had attained fearlessness.
They were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who had measured the roots of goodness planted by the Buddha and entered the Mahāyāna,
namely: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nimiṃdhara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharaṇīdhara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhūmipati,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sattvadhara, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Parṣanmaṇḍaladhara.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ālokamati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Atikrāntamati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vṛddhimati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Priyadarśana, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudarśana, and the Bodhisattva Darśanavat.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvārthadarśin, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvamaṅgalya,
and all the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa sat together in the assembly, with Maitreya at their head.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, in the early morning, took up his robe and bowl and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"Last night I dreamed that a Tathāgata was seated at the site of enlightenment; I then immediately prostrated at the feet of this World-Honored One, and the Buddha, with his golden right hand, stroked the crown of my head and spoke these words: 'Subhūti!'"
"Today you shall hear the Dharma that you have never heard before.
"World-Honored One!
What is this prior omen?"
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! That these sons and daughters of good family hear this rare and unprecedented Dharma is a prior omen.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go to the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in due order.”
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, you know the time."

Having received the World-Honored One’s permission, the Venerable Subhūti immediately entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in sequence. Arriving at the house of a certain elder, he stood silently at the middle gate to beg for food.

At that time, there was a woman in the house who came out from within; she was foremost in her exquisite beauty and supreme in her loveliness, most dignified and possessed of great majesty. She adorned herself with various necklaces and ornaments, which, as the precious jewels brushed against one another, produced wondrous sounds.
Having arrived outside, he said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable One,
for what reason do you stand at the middle gate?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
I am standing at the gate for the purpose of begging for alms."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Do you still harbor the notion of begging for alms?"
"Venerable Subhūti, do you still not understand the perception of food?
Subhūti replied, "Sister!"
I understand the perception of food: this body is a collection of the impurities of father and mother, nurtured by food and drink; therefore, it cannot exist apart from food.
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Have you not now realized the cessation of ignorance, up to and including the realization of the cessation of birth, old age, and death?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
I have realized cessation."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Is there bodily nutriment that nourishes and sustains within cessation?"
Subhūti said: "Sister! In cessation, there is no further dharma."
The woman said:
"Virtuous One!
If, once extinguished, there is no further dharma, how can the Venerable Subhūti say that the body is nourished by food?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
One who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation eliminates all sensation and perception; yet, having emerged from that absorption, the body is sustained and nourished."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Does this cessation itself have arising and ceasing?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
As for this cessation, it is without arising and without cessation; this is ultimate cessation."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
If this is cessation, ultimate cessation, how can one nourish the body?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
It is for the sake of nourishing their bodies that the World-Honored One’s śrāvakas wander about begging for food."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti! The World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost among those who practice the absence of contention."
Subhūti said: “Sister, it is as you have said.”
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti! Does one who is without contention have either practice or non-practice?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
This one who is without contention has neither practice nor non-practice."
The woman said,
"Venerable Subhūti!
For what purpose do you beg for alms?"
Subhūti said: “Sister!

I, who am a mendicant, do not go begging for food for the sake of nourishing the body; rather, I go begging for food for the sake of sustaining a frail life and for the purpose of eliminating all sensations.”
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Are you still being led by the various sensations?"
Subhūti said: "I am no longer led by sensations; because I have eliminated sensation, I go for alms.
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
The practice of non-contention is neither discordant nor unequal. Why is this?

In practicing non-contention, there is no experience of suffering; yet this non-contention is not associated with body or mind. This non-contention does not give rise to pleasure or non-pleasure, and this non-contention does not give rise to dispute."
"Venerable Subhūti!

The World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost among those who practice the absence of contention (*araṇā*). For what reason and by what causes is 'absence of contention' called 'absence of contention'?
Subhūti replied:
"Sister! One who is free from contention has no objective realms and is detached from the dust of desire.
The woman said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
Can this ‘absence of contention’ bring about freedom from desire?
Subhūti replied:
"Sister! This one who is free from contention cannot be separated from desire.
The woman said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
For what reason do you say that the absence of contention can bring about freedom from the dust of desire?”
Subhūti said: "Sister!
It is by way of verbal expression that it is called 'non-contention'."
The woman said:
“Venerable Subhūti! Can that which is ‘without contention’ (araṇā) indeed be described?”
Subhūti said: "Sister! This state of one who is without contention is ineffable."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
If that which is without contention is inexpressible, for what reason is it called 'without contention'?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks of the śrāvaka disciples using provisional names."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
If there is a provisional name, then there is dispute; if there is dispute, then there is perversion; if there is perversion, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa."
Subhūti said: "Sister!
What is the dharma of a śramaṇa?"
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
To be without words, without dispute, and without inversion—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa."
Furthermore, one does not discriminate between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma as being the dharma of a śramaṇa;
nor does one discriminate between recollection and non-recollection as being the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be free from all attachments is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Neither being within the sphere of perception nor being outside the sphere of perception is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
neither being defiled nor bound, nor being undefiled and unbound, is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be without mind and free from mental consciousness is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Contentment is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
fewness of desires and the severing of greed are the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be free from all longing, neither moving nor initiating, yet not being unmoving or uninitiating, is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be free from all objective spheres because there is nothing to be grasped is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to be free from the māra of the aggregates because there is no defiled attachment is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to sever the māra of the fetters so that they do not arise again is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To remain far removed from the Māra of death and to be free from all agitation is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to contemplate and not associate with the celestial Māras is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
that all dharmas are empty and without defilement is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be without ideation and to be free from all ideations is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to be without aspiration and without attachment is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
not to course within the three realms and to be free from all ideations is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Guarding the sense faculties is the Dharma of a śramaṇa;
remaining detached from the sense bases is the Dharma of a śramaṇa;
skillfully self-subduing and abandoning all conceptual proliferation is the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Quiescence and non-arising are the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be without attachment and without the impulse to act is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to be without "I" or "mine," and without high or low, is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To be untainted by contact is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to remain far removed from worldly dharmas is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
to skillfully understand the aggregates and comprehend the nature of phenomena as they lead to their destination is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Because all elements are without elements, without intimacy, and without obstruction, this is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
because it is free from conditioned phenomena, this is the dharma of a śramaṇa;
because all dharmas are like space, this is the dharma of a śramaṇa.

While these teachings on the dharmas of a śramaṇa were being spoken, thirty sons of gods among the deities assembled at the middle gate to hear the Dharma attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.
Furthermore, there were five devaputras who, being inclined toward the profound Dharma, heard this woman’s eloquence and gave rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti conceived a sense of wonder and thought to himself:
"Since this woman possesses such eloquence, she must certainly be a transformation of the Tathāgata; of this there is no doubt."
At that time, this woman, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Subhūti, spoke these words: "Venerable Subhūti!
You have had this thought, yet there is no doubt at all that this woman is a transformation of the Tathāgata."
"Venerable One!
It is exactly so, exactly as you have conceived it. Why is this?"
The Tathāgata knows suchness, and I also know suchness; for this reason, the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata awakens to suchness, I also awaken to suchness; for this reason, the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s form is suchness, my form is also suchness; for this reason, the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the same as my suchness of consciousness, then for this reason the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s suchness and the suchness of all sentient beings are the same as my suchness—suchness being one and the same—for this reason the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s suchness and the suchness of all phenomena are the same as my suchness—suchness being one and the same—for this reason the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s suchness is not otherwise, and my suchness is not otherwise—if this suchness is eternally such and never otherwise—for this reason the Tathāgata transforms me.
If the Tathāgata’s suchness is without birth and without cessation, my suchness is likewise without birth and without cessation; for this reason the Tathāgata transforms me.

Whether it be the Tathāgata’s suchness, the suchness of the Tathāgata’s transformation, my suchness, the suchness of all sentient beings, or the suchness of all phenomena—this suchness is eternally true, non-different, unchanging, and immutable. It contains nothing within it; this suchness abides thus in all phenomena. For this reason, the Tathāgata transforms me.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again asked:
"Sister! Do you know my mind through the power of the Buddha?"
"Is it known through one's own power?
The woman replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!"

Whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or rishis possessing the five supernatural powers, when they know the minds of sentient beings or the minds of others, they all know those other minds through the power of the Buddha.
Why is this? All that these [beings] practice is known through the power of the Buddha’s ability to know the minds of others.
The Venerable Subhūti also knows the minds of others by means of the Buddha’s power.
Venerable Subhūti!
It is like how a person with clear vision perceives forms by means of the light of the sun, the moon, fire, precious jewels, lightning, and stars.
Venerable Subhūti!
"In this world, those who possess knowledge of others' minds while being shrouded by ignorance all do so because the Tathāgata knows their minds.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said,
"Sister, you should explain to me how you have attained such eloquence."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Suppose someone were to ask a transformation being created by the Tathāgata:"
“Who are you? How should this emanated being answer? Subhūti said:
"Sister! There is nothing to answer.
The woman said:
“Venerable Subhūti!
All dharmas are likewise thus; they are all illusory manifestations. Having known this, there is nothing to answer.”
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!
If someone were to ask you:
'Are you an ordinary person?'"
"Is this a trainee (śaikṣa) or an arhat?
Having been asked thus, how would you answer?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:
"How shall I answer this sister?
Immediately, Subhūti heard a voice from the air saying:
"Venerable Subhūti!
You have something attained, something understood, and something realized; for this reason you are called an Arhat. Answer this sister!"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, having heard the voice from the air, immediately replied to the woman:
"Sister! I am not an ordinary person, nor am I a learner (śaikṣa), nor am I an arhat."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
By what name do you hold yourself?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
Just as the Tathāgata’s transformation maintains a provisional name, I likewise maintain a provisional name."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Are you not an Arhat who has severed all outflows?"
"The Tathāgata has declared that you are foremost in practicing non-contention;
you should receive offerings. Subhūti said, "Sister!"
"I am not an arhat; I have not exhausted all outflows; I do not practice the foremost state of non-contention;
nor am I one worthy of offerings. The woman said: "Venerable Subhūti!..."
"Why do you speak falsely? Subhūti said,
"Sister!"
If I were now to grant that an Arhat—one whose outflows are exhausted, who practices the foremost state of non-contention, and who is worthy of offerings—exists, it would be a falsehood;
yet I grant nothing at all. Therefore, I am neither speaking falsely nor speaking truly.
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Do you not now deceive these devaputras who have gathered at this gate and perceived the Noble Truths?"
Subhūti said: "Sister!
One who has seen the Noble Truths cannot be deceived."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Do you perceive the Noble Truths?"
Then Subhūti replied,
“I have seen her.
The woman said:
“Venerable One!
If one perceives the Noble Truths, they are not called ‘Noble Truths. Why is this?
"There is no one capable of seeing the noble truths.
The woman said,
"Venerable Subhūti!"
“Is it not that you have seen the Noble Truths? Subhūti said,
“Sister!”
I speak neither of the real nor of the unreal.
Sister!
I do not perceive the unreal; how much less could I perceive the real?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again asked the woman: "Sister!
What does one who has seen the Noble Truths say?"
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
One who perceives the Noble Truths does not perceive the names of any dharmas; one who perceives the Noble Truths perceives the names of perversions."
Subhūti said: "Sister!
For what reason do you speak such words?"
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!

If there are inverted views that give rise to the fetters (saṃyojana), once the Noble Truths have been seen, they no longer arise. For this reason it is said: 'One who sees inverted views sees the Noble Truths.'"
At that time, the devas manifested their forms, paid homage to the Venerable Subhūti, and spoke these words:

"Venerable Subhūti, you have gained great benefit; by hearing such eloquence from this sister, you will cause all sentient beings to gain great and wholesome benefit through hearing the Dharma, believing it, and understanding it."
"Why is this? For one who does not possess extensive understanding, there is no liberation; for one who does not possess extensive understanding, there is bondage. What, then, would be understood?
At that time, the woman said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Do you not beg for food? Do you not eat?
Subhūti said, "Sister!..."
"Today, having heard this Dharma-satisfaction, I have no desire for food.
Sister!
To be greedy for food and drink gives rise to sorrow; it is not the pursuit of the Dharma."
To seek gain, offerings, and praise is not to seek the Dharma;
to seek physical comfort is not to seek the Dharma;
to cherish and protect one's mind, body, and life is not to seek the Dharma.
"Even receiving praise such as 'Excellent! is not seeking the Dharma.
Subhūti said, "Sister!"
"You have now further asked: 'How do sons and daughters of good family correctly seek the Dharma?
The woman said:
'Venerable Subhūti!'"

If one accepts evil desires, this is not seeking the Dharma; if one seeks neither the eye nor forms, this person seeks the Dharma; if one seeks neither the ear nor sounds, neither the nose nor odors, neither the tongue nor flavors, neither the body nor tangibles, nor the mind nor mental phenomena, this person seeks the Dharma.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!
If one does not seek the aggregates (*skandha*), does not seek the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and does not seek the elements (*dhātu*), that person seeks the Dharma;
if one does not seek the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), that person seeks the Dharma.
"If one does not seek after any objective realm, that person seeks the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said:
"Sister!"
"You should repent your transgression; I now wish to depart.
The woman said, "Venerable Subhūti!"
Just as the earth element has no repentance,
so too, O Venerable Subhūti,
is the mind; like the earth element, it should not repent.
Just as the element of water has no regret, so too is the mind; being identical to the element of water, it should not regret.
Just as the elements of fire, wind, and space have no regret, so too is the mind; being identical to the element of space, it should not regret.
Venerable Subhūti!
Just as a bridge, a boat, a float, or a royal highway has no need for repentance, Venerable Subhūti!
The mind is likewise; like a bridge, a boat, a float, or a royal highway, it should not repent.
"Venerable Subhūti!
It is ordinary persons who repent, not the noble ones!

If one gives rise to anger, then there is repentance; but for those who are without hatred, without entanglement, without resentment, without contention, and who do not give rise to the fetters—such people as these should not repent."
Venerable Subhūti!
Just as there is extinction because fire is blazing, and no extinction when it does not blaze;
so it is, Venerable Subhūti!
"If the fetters are blazing, then there is remorse; if the fetters are extinguished, then there is no remorse.
At that time, Subhūti spoke again to the woman, saying:
"Sister!"
"What do you seek or aspire to, that you are able to roar such a lion's roar?
The woman said,
"Venerable Subhūti!"
If there is something sought, one cannot roar the lion’s roar.
Venerable Subhūti!
If there is nothing sought, one can roar the lion’s roar.

Why is this? If there is anything sought, that is precisely "existence. If there is existence, there is no lion's roar. Those who possess the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) have something to seek; those who hold views of a creator have no lion's roar.
"Venerable Subhūti!
Regarding what you just said, 'Sister, where are you going?'—
Venerable Subhūti!"
"If someone were to ask you, 'Where have you gone?
Have you attained liberation through the mind of the exhaustion of outflows and the realization of non-arising?
what would you say? Subhūti replied:
"Sister! If there is something to be sought, there will be no liberation.
The woman said:
“Venerable Subhūti!

If you seek in this manner, you will exhaust all outflows and attain the mind free from outflows; if you proceed in this manner, it is proceeding toward liberation, it is proceeding toward the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said: "Sister!
You have set out upon the Great Vehicle without doubt; by the signs of your practice, it is certain that you are destined for the unsurpassed Great Vehicle."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Do you know the Mahāyāna?"
"Speak of the characteristics of practice. Subhūti said:
"Sister!"
"If the śrāvakas have not heard the Mahāyāna, they are unable to know or explain the characteristics of the various practices.
Sister!
I now request you to explain all the characteristics of the practices of the Mahāyāna."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti! As for the Great Vehicle, it is called that which has neither unity nor difference."
"Venerable Subhūti!
Just as the palaces of the sun and moon, being sustained by the gods, do not remain stationary in space but move swiftly without obstruction, providing light for all sentient beings."
Venerable Subhūti!

It is likewise for those great beings who are oriented toward the Mahāyāna; they are thus unimpeded and unattached, practicing the six pāramitās without dwelling upon them, acting as the light of the Dharma for all sentient beings.
“Venerable Subhūti!

Just as when the precious wheel of a Wheel-turning King moves, the fourfold army follows; and just as when the Wheel-turning King travels through the four continents, people see him and find him pleasing, giving rise to a heart of reverence—yet this Wheel-turning King has no evil intent and constantly gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness.”
Venerable Subhūti!

It is likewise for those great beings who are oriented toward the Mahāyāna; wherever they may go—whether in villages, towns, settlements, cities, or royal palaces—they give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and do not engage in any partial conduct.
“Venerable Subhūti!
The Great Vehicle is called Great Wisdom; it is that which is revered by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and wise mahāpuruṣas. For this reason, it is named the Great Vehicle.”
This is inexhaustible wisdom, because it is without arising or ceasing;
this is uninterrupted wisdom, because it does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas;
this is inclusive wisdom, because it does not sever the lineage of the Dharma.
This is the wisdom of protection, for it does not sever the lineage of the Sangha;
this is the wisdom of vastness, for it transforms and guides immeasurable sentient beings;
this is the wisdom of skillful retention, for it is never interrupted.
This is the wisdom of skillful action, because of the six pāramitās;
this is the wisdom of skillful gathering, because of the four means of integration;
this is the wisdom of skillful correspondence, because of approaching through the noble path.
This is the wisdom of excellent cultivation, because it never forgets or loses the bodhicitta through right mindfulness;
this is the wisdom of excellent stabilization, because of the mind of great compassion;
this is the wisdom of excellent progression, because of omniscience.
This is the wisdom that is free from all fears, for it subdues all Māras;
this is the wisdom that is free from darkness, for it is the great torch of intelligence;
this is the wisdom of great wealth, for it brings to fulfillment all roots of goodness.
This is the wisdom that is revered, for it is honored by all devas and the world.
This is the wisdom that cannot be overcome, because of all heterodox teachers;
this is the wisdom that is difficult to understand, because of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is the wisdom of purity, for the sake of those who lack faith;
this is the wisdom of loving-kindness and compassion, for the sake of those who harbor malice and harm others;
this is the wisdom of generosity, for the sake of those who are stingy and possessive.
This is the wisdom of ethical discipline, for the sake of those who violate the precepts;
this is the wisdom of patience, for the sake of those who harbor anger;
this is the wisdom of diligence, for the sake of those who are indolent.
This is the wisdom of meditative concentration for those with distracted minds;
this is the wisdom of great insight for those lacking wisdom;
this is the wisdom of great wealth for those who are impoverished.
This is the wisdom of peace and bliss because it concerns those who suffer;
this is the wisdom of joy because it concerns those who are wise and intelligent.
For these reasons, it is called the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said:
"Sister! You have well explained the characteristics of the various practices of the Mahāyāna."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Even if I were to spend an eon, or more than an eon, praising and speaking of the Mahāyāna, I would not reach its limit."
"Venerable Subhūti!
These immeasurable practices of the Great Vehicle likewise have immeasurable characteristics. Subhūti said:
"Sister! You reproach me; why does the Venerable Subhūti go for alms?
Sister!"
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, likewise begs for food; can you reproach the Tathāgata for begging for food?
The woman said, "Venerable Subhūti!"
"Do you know by what skillful means the Tathāgata goes on his almsround?
You cannot say. Subhūti replied:
"Sister! By what skillful means does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, go on his almsround?
The woman replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
The Buddha’s vision is perfected; because he is free from faults regarding twenty matters, he goes on almsround.
What are these twenty?

The Tathāgata goes on almsround to manifest a physical body; if there are sentient beings who see the Tathāgata’s body endowed with the thirty-two marks, those beings, upon seeing these physical characteristics, will give rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. This is called the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the first perfection, being free from faults, and thus going on almsround.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

When the Tathāgata enters villages, towns, cities, royal palaces, or royal courts, the blind see forms, the deaf hear sounds, the mentally deranged regain right mindfulness, the naked obtain clothing, the hungry obtain food, and the thirsty obtain drink;
there is not a single sentient being who is oppressed by greed, hatred, or delusion."

At that time, sentient beings each gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and conceived of [the Tathāgata] as their father and mother; upon seeing the Tathāgata entering villages, towns, cities, royal palaces, and kingdoms, these sentient beings all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti,

when the Tathāgata enters villages, towns, cities, royal palaces, or the abodes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, they follow after the Tathāgata out of a desire to make offerings.
At that time, by the power of the Buddha, all people saw the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors making offerings to the Buddha.

When these sentient beings saw such things as these in the body of the Tathāgata, they were struck with wonder and amazement, exclaiming that it was unprecedented, and they gave rise to the mind set on supreme, true, and perfect enlightenment.
It is because he perceives this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.

Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, there are immeasurable sentient beings who, possessing sovereign power over fiefs, wealth, and royal stations, become negligent, arrogant, and conceited; seeing the Tathāgata begging for alms, they conceive such thoughts as these:

"He renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning King to leave the household life and attain the Way; he abandoned pride and arrogance to beg for food from the poor and lowly. We, too, should subdue our hearts of pride and haughtiness."
Having seen this, he gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

When the Tathāgata goes on almsround, the various devas of majestic power behold the body of the Tathāgata as neither oppressed by hunger or thirst nor emaciated; he goes for alms solely out of compassion for all sentient beings. We, too, should go for alms for the sake of sentient beings.
Having seen this, they give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is for the sake of this principle that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

There are sentient beings who, being indolent and lazy, do not go to where the Buddha is; yet they desire to see the Tathāgata, circumambulate him, and pay him homage. For this reason, the Tathāgata enters villages, market towns, cities, and royal palaces, so that these sentient beings may naturally behold the Buddha, the Tathāgata. Having beheld him, their hearts give rise to joy. Once these sentient beings have attained such joy, they immediately resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
It is for the sake of this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.

Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, if there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha with their eyes, immediately become free from delusion—even if they see the Tathāgata for but a single thought-moment—these sentient beings will gradually and successively proceed toward Nirvāṇa. Because he can produce these causes and conditions, the Tathāgata begs for food.
Seeing this meaning, the Tathāgata goes for alms.

Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, when the Tathāgata enters villages, towns, marketplaces, cities, or royal palaces, those beings who are bound and imprisoned immediately attain liberation; these beings then give rise to this thought:
"By the power of the Tathāgata, I have attained liberation.
Thus, these sentient beings conceive a sense of gratitude toward the Tathāgata and resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti,
there may be sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the praise of all the merits of the Tathāgata, give rise to joy in their hearts and form this thought:
"How shall we provide food for the Buddha?

Furthermore, there are women in households who are protected by their parents, or protected by their brothers and sisters, or guarded by their paternal aunts, mothers-in-law, or husbands; such individuals are unable to offer food to the Buddha. Therefore, when the Tathāgata enters a village, town, city, kingdom, or royal palace, those who see the Tathāgata feel joy in their hearts; they leap for joy with delight and receive peace and happiness. Having offered food to the Buddha, they give rise to the mind of unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is for the sake of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

The Four World-Protecting Kings present their bowls to the Tathāgata, which he holds in his own hand. If a poor being wishes to give a small gift, they see the Tathāgata’s bowl already full; yet if one who possesses great wealth and a noble fief wishes to give much, they see the Buddha’s bowl as not yet full. Such persons, desiring to fill the Buddha’s bowl to its capacity, offer their gifts and subsequently resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti,
the Tathāgata offers the food in his alms-bowl to the entire Saṅgha, yet that food neither increases nor decreases.

At that time, many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, seeing such supernatural power in the Tathāgata’s bowl, gave rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because he perceives this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

When the Tathāgata’s bowl is filled with both pure and impure food, though there are hundreds of thousands of flavors, each flavor remains distinct and does not blend together, as if they were in separate vessels; it is the same even when they are contained within this single bowl."
At that time, many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, seeing such supernatural power of the Tathāgata, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, the body of the Tathāgata is a single integrated whole;

its interior is not empty, being like a diamond. This body of the Tathāgata has no stomach or intestines, nor does it have excrement or urine, yet he still goes out to beg for food. Seeing him eat, one sees that the food he consumes does not enter [his body].

At that time, the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors of majestic power, beholding the Tathāgata’s body, its true dharma-nature, and his supernormal powers, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
It is because he perceives this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for alms.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, if there are sentient beings—
whether many or few, whether excellent or not— who give to the Tathāgata, their merit will be boundless, even unto nirvāṇa.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.

Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, remains constantly in meditative concentration and does not arise from it, yet he still practices begging for food. At that time, many beings of great majesty—the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors—seeing the Tathāgata practicing begging for food while remaining unmoved in concentration, give rise to this thought:
"Be certain and free from doubt: it is for the sake of sentient beings that I proceed to beg for alms, not for the sake of food.
Upon seeing this supernatural power, he gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
It is because of seeing this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti,
if the Tathāgata were not to practice begging for food, or if he were not to eat, there might be some people who have gone forth into the Buddha-dharma and give rise to such a thought:
"We too shall not go on almsround, and we too shall not eat.
These people will then become emaciated from hunger and thirst, and they will be unable to attain superhuman wisdom.
It is because he perceives this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, it is because he properly maintains the noble lineages that the Tathāgata begs for food; it is because he perceives this meaning that the Tathāgata begs for food.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!
Out of compassion for the bhikṣus of future generations, the Tathāgata begs for alms.
In the final age, there will be brahmins and householders who lack faith and respect, and they will say these words:"
"Why do you not go on alms-round, when the World-honored One does not go on alms-round?
If the Tathāgata were to go on alms-round, these brahmins and elders would think:
"The World-honored One originally went on alms-round; why do you not go on alms-round?"
"We should give.
Furthermore, it is the natural law for all Tathāgatas to practice begging, and they praise the act of seeking alms.
Seeing this significance, the Tathāgata begs for food.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!

If wealthy householders, sons of householders, or those of great nobility and status go forth in the Buddha-dharma, they may give rise to a sense of shame and be unable to beg for food, thinking to themselves:
'How can we, who belong to noble clans and great families, having already gone forth, go from house to house to beg for alms?'"
"Such persons as these follow the example of the Great Virtuous One, the Tathāgata of majestic power, in going on alms-round.
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata goes on alms-round.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!..."
The Tathāgata conforms to all worldly activities.

Why is this? Wherever sentient beings are ripened, there the Tathāgata follows along. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is not oppressed by hunger or thirst; he is without greed and without attachment, nor does he engage in frivolous play. He has no evil desires and makes no accumulations.
Venerable Subhūti!
Regarding what has been said above and other such matters, the Tathāgata perceives these immeasurable skillful means and thus practices begging for alms.
Venerable Subhūti!
"Seeing these twenty matters free from faults and afflictions, the Tathāgata begs for alms.
The woman said,
"Venerable Subhūti!"
"Can one practice alms-gathering through such skillful means?
With such great compassion and such purity, should one not be worthy of receiving offerings?
Subhūti replied:
"Sister! I am powerless.
Sister!"
Sister, it is just as hares, cats, and jackals cannot adorn themselves as the lion, the king of beasts; they cannot perform the lion’s gait nor let out the lion’s roar.
Sister!
"All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise unable to manifest the Tathāgata’s majestic deportment, skillful means, and great compassion.

While this daughter was speaking these words concerning the Tathāgata’s skillful means of begging for alms, two hundred and eighty people from her own household, its attendants, and other families who had entered to listen to the Dharma, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again asked the woman:
"Sister! Where is your husband now?"
The woman said,
"Venerable Subhūti!
My husband is not merely one!"
Why is this? Venerable Subhūti!
If there are sentient beings who delight in being disciplined through the skillful means of adornment according to their desires, they are all my husbands.
Subhūti said: "Sister!
What is the nature of one who delights in the skillful means of adornment?"
The woman said:

"If there are sentient beings who require various pleasures and desires, I shall bestow upon those beings all that they desire, and thereafter exhort them to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path."
Subhūti said: "Sister!
The Tathāgata does not permit the enjoyment of any desires."
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
As the Buddha has taught: "

"O bhikṣus! Regarding all your robes, alms bowls, food, drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness—whether from the homes of your relatives, the homes from which you beg, the places where you reside, or the presence of your friends, preceptors (upādhyāya), and teachers (ācārya)—by drawing near to and making offerings to them, you increase all roots of goodness and extinguish all unwholesome dharmas, O bhikṣus!"
"This is what I have heard. Subhūti said, "Sister!"
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
For this reason, the Tathāgata permits delighting in all desires."
Subhūti said: "Sister!
How many sentient beings are there who are disciplined by these ornaments of aspiration and skillful means?"
The woman said:

"Venerable Subhūti, you may be able to count all the physical forms within the trichiliocosm and reach their limit; yet, if one were to count my skillful means of adornment for taming sentient beings, one would never reach their limit."
Subhūti said: "Sister!
What is it like for sentient beings who possess desire?"
The woman said, "Venerable Subhūti!

If there are sentient beings who delight in proceeding toward the Brahma world, I shall bestow upon all such sentient beings immeasurable dhyānas; once they have experienced the joy and bliss of these dhyānas, I will thereafter exhort them to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path."

If there are sentient beings who take pleasure in seeking the state of Śakra Devānām Indra, [the Buddha] first provides these beings with the pleasures of Śakra, and only thereafter exhorts them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the pleasures of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), I shall first provide those beings with the pleasures of the World-Protectors, and only thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*).

If there are sentient beings who delight in the pleasures of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas, I shall provide them with the pleasures of devas up to the pleasures of mahoragas, and only thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings whose aspirations and inclinations are directed toward the kingdom of a wheel-turning monarch, I first grant them the pleasures of the kingdom of a wheel-turning monarch, and only thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the pleasures of a minor king, I likewise bestow upon them the pleasures of a minor king, and thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in becoming elders, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras, I grant them the pleasures of being elders, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras, and thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the pleasures of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles, I provide them with the pleasures of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles, and only then exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in flowers, incense, powdered incense, unguents, banners, pennants, precious canopies, and various garments, I shall provide them with flowers, incense, powdered incense, unguents, banners, pennants, precious canopies, and garments according to their desires; only after they have received these pleasures will I exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and other such rare treasures, I shall provide them with the pleasure of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and precious jewels, and only thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who delight in music such as drums, conchs, lutes, reed organs, flutes, pipes, singing, dancing,
and instrumental performances— O Venerable Subhūti!
Following these sentient beings, I shall grant them everything they hope for, seek, and desire, and thereafter exhort them to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
Subhūti said: "Sister!
These five desires obstruct the Noble Path; how, then, can the five desires tame sentient beings?"
At that time, the two sons of the elder outside the gate had already been tamed by this daughter’s skillful means of joyful adornment.
Those two sons of the elder then spoke to the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
You should not now use your own wisdom to discriminate or select the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Venerable One!
It is like a small lamp that is extinguished by a single breath. Venerable Subhūti!

It is likewise for the sons and daughters of good family who study the Śrāvaka-yāna; with their limited wisdom-light, as soon as a single thought of desire arises, it is immediately extinguished and lost.
"Venerable Subhūti!
What do you think?
If, at the time of the kalpa-conflagration, there were a mass of blazing fires, could one extinguish them by blowing upon them with the mouth?"
Subhūti said: “If even the waters of hundreds of thousands of great oceans could not extinguish it, how much less so a single breath?”
“Venerable Subhūti!

It is likewise with the illumination of a bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom; even if one were to experience the pleasures of the five desires for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it could not extinguish the illumination of that bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom.”
"Venerable Subhūti!

Suppose a poor person falls ill, and a physician prescribes medicinal decoctions that are bitter, astringent, sweet, or sour, and which are inexpensive and easy to obtain. At that time, because the patient’s body is suffering, they take these bitter, astringent, sweet, and sour medicines; and because of their poverty, they endure hunger and thirst to be freed from the illness."
Venerable Subhūti!

It is the same for those sons and daughters of good family who study the vehicle of the śrāvakas: by practicing the dhūta qualities and dignified conduct, through their correct practice they have few desires and know contentment; because of their ascetic austerities, their dwelling in forest hermitages, and their acceptance of both coarse and choice food, as well as having few acquaintances, they undergo various sufferings and afflictions, and only thereafter do they attain liberation without grasping.
"Venerable Subhūti!
It is the same for those who study the Śrāvaka vehicle through such skillful means and attain liberation; it is like a poor man treating his illness.
"Venerable Subhūti! [he continued.]

It is just as when a consecrated Kṣatriya king falls ill, and the king’s skilled physicians prescribe for him medicines of excellent color, fragrance, and flavor; these enter his mouth and body, bringing him peace and happiness. They also present him with exquisite delicacies fit for a king, and offer all kinds of flowers, incense, powdered incense, ointments, and scattered perfumes. Furthermore, they provide music, song, and dance to praise him, so that he may experience joy. To ensure that the Great King is free from sorrow and suffering, these skilled physicians entertain him in such various ways, enabling him to be liberated from his illness.
Venerable Subhūti! It is just the same:

there are many bodhisattvas who, by means of the skillful means of adornment with joy, experience all the pleasures of the five desires, and only thereafter attain the realization of the unsurpassed, right path.
"Venerable Subhūti!
You should know that by means of this skillful method one treats the illness of a consecrated Kṣatriya king; the wisdom and understanding of a bodhisattva is likewise."
"Venerable Subhūti! The five desires have no root and no place of abiding;

all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is likewise, having no original place of abiding. This all-knowledge knows for itself what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Regarding the pleasures of the five desires, it neither finds pleasure nor finds lack of pleasure, because it is solitary and without companion. Thus, this all-knowledge possesses no merit, because there is nothing to be attained."
One who attains this patience knows for themselves: "What is the Path?
What is not the Path?

Since the virtues of the five desires are empty and all-knowledge is empty, such a person who has attained patience does not pursue the five desires; they personally perceive the faults and afflictions of the five desires and censure them.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked the son of the householder,
"Who is your relative? Thereupon,
the son of the householder joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and spoke this verse to the girl:
"These are my parents; my kinsmen and friends who gave me medicine;
these are those who cut off rebirth in the evil realms; these are my unsurpassed venerables.
These are my great benefactors; they have also instructed and transformed me."
Because he exhorted me, he severed all my suffering;
for my sake, he preached the sublime Dharma, explaining all principles.
I have received swift peace and happiness, and he has also urged me toward non-contention.
Just as a fish, for the sake of food, Is caught and pulled by a hook, So too is the pursuit of pleasure; It ensnares us.
Just as a bird, for the sake of food, Is held fast by a net,
My skillful means are likewise so:
having fallen into wisdom, I am like one bitten by a snake who uses poison to extinguish poison;
desire and hatred are also thus—using poison to eliminate poison.
Just as when a person is burned by fire, they use fire again to cauterize and remove [the wound], so too it is with the burning of the fetters:
liberation from the fetters occurs through the very cause of those fetters.
I have already known the True Dharma; I no longer require sensual desire.
"Ordinary people desire [sensual] things, and do not desire the path to enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti said: "Sister!"
With these skillful means adorned by joy, whom do you seek to discipline?
Is it a son of good family,
or a daughter of good family?
The woman said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
If one does not employ the skillful means of adorning with this joy, one cannot transform and guide all sentient beings."
"Venerable Subhūti!
The minds of women are characterized by much craving and attachment, whereas those of men are not.
"Venerable sir! [he replied.]
"I have subdued many women through skillful means adorned with pleasure,
not men. Subhūti said, "Sister!"
"You are a woman's body; how can you subdue women?

At that time, this goddess used her supernatural power to transform her body into that of a vigorous man of thirty-two years of age, with a handsome and wondrous complexion, pure white and radiant, possessing supreme majesty and virtue. Having adorned herself with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, she said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"With such a physical form as this, one subdues women."
Subhūti asked,
"Are you now a woman or a man?
She replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
Are you an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or are you one in training (*śaikṣa*)? Subhūti replied:
“Good son! I am neither an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), nor am I one in training (*śaikṣa*).
He then replied again:
"I am likewise neither male nor female.
Subhūti said, "If you are neither male nor female, by what name are you known?"
He replied: "Venerable Subhūti!
You are neither an ordinary person nor one in training; how then do you bear this name?"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:
"This is a Great Bodhisattva of profound wisdom; I should answer him, 'He is an Arhat.'"
At that time, this son of good family, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the venerable Subhūti, spoke to the venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"You should courageously advance and grant him the status of an Arhat; do not fear his words or questions.
Subhūti said, "O son of good family!"
"I am an arhat; all outflows have been exhausted.
He then asked again:
"Venerable Subhūti!..."
Regarding the past, future, and present, what outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted?
If they were exhausted in the past, the past would not be inexhaustible;
if they have not yet arrived in the future, there is likewise no exhaustion.
"The present does not abide, nor does it have an end.
Subhūti said, "Noble son!"
"I am truly not fit to engage in mutual discourse with you; it is now time for me to go begging for food and eat, lest I miss the proper hour.
At that moment, this son of good family entered the samādhi called "Manifesting All Buddha-fields."

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti immediately beheld immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddha-fields. In some he saw the Buddha-sun at the time of its first rising; in some, at the time of the morning meal; in some, at the time of the midday meal; in some, at the time when the *gandī* was struck; in some, he saw the Saṃgha seated; in some, the Saṃgha eating; in some, them washing their bowls; in some, he saw the middle of the day; in some, the afternoon; in some, past the afternoon; in some, the setting of the sun; in some, the first watch of the night; in some, the middle watch; in some, the last watch; and in some, he saw no sun or moon, as they were illuminated by the radiance of the bodies [of the Buddhas].
At that time, this son of good family said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Behold now! Behold now!"
"When do you wish to eat?
Observe now: how much time remains?
Subhūti said:
“Good son! I shall now eat according to the time of Jambudvīpa, not according to the time of other Buddha-fields.
At that moment, by means of his supernatural power, this good son caused midday to appear as the hour for a light meal, and spoke to Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Observe this sun; how many hours does it remain?
Venerable Subhūti, out of affection and friendship, asked thus:
“Good son! What is your name? Speak it now. He replied:
“Venerable Subhūti!
For what purpose do you use my name?
Venerable Subhūti!”
"You have asked the World-Honored One; he shall explain it for you.
Venerable sir!
All names are non-names."
"Why is this? Because all conceptual constructions (vikalpa) lack reality. If conceptual constructions lack reality, they are said to exist only by way of conventional designations. Subhūti said:
“Good son! Is even the name ‘omniscience’ a false conceptualization and not real?
He replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!
This, too, is a conceptual construction and lacks reality. Why is this so?
"The name 'Omniscience' is immeasurable and boundless; in each and every Buddha-field, it is spoken of by different names.
Subhūti said, "Noble son!"
"What is the name of this omniscience? He replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!"

There are some buddha-fields named *Sarvajñā-vibhakti-prabhā* (Light of the Differentiation of All-Knowledge), or named *Samantāvabhāsa* (Universal Illumination), or again named *Sarvajñā-saṃdarśana* (Manifestation of All-Knowledge), or named *Vardhamāna-vīrya* (Increasing Valor), or named *Mahāprabha* (Great Light), or named *Pratyutpanna* (The Present), or named *Dharanidhara* (Holding the Earth), or named *Mahāvinirjita* (Great Conquest), or named *Mahāsamanta* (Great Universality).
"Venerable Subhūti!

Just as 'all-knowledge' has immeasurable names, so too does 'form' have immeasurable names; likewise, 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'volitional formations,' and 'consciousness' each have immeasurable names. Furthermore, the elements, the sense bases, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, and all the dharmas that assist the path—each of these has immeasurable names in every buddha-field."
"Venerable One!
What is the reality of this name?
Venerable Subhūti!"
"By this expedient means, you should know that all names are not names, and all conceptualizations of names are not real.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti exclaimed:
"The great householders, brahmins, and others of Rājagṛha have gained a great and wholesome benefit, for such an Arhat dwells here as their guest."
He spoke again to the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Are you now able to know the World-Honored One, the Arhat?
Subhūti replied:

“Good son! I shall now speak according to what I know: if there are those who uphold the precepts, practice wholesome dharmas, and skillfully enter meditative concentration with an undisturbed mind, these are called those who are worthy of offerings by the world.”
He replied,
"Venerable Subhūti, that which you have described as 'worthy of offerings' is likewise not complete. Subhūti said:
“Good son! You should now explain what it means to be ‘worthy of offerings’ (arhat).
He replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!
If one lacks great compassion toward all sentient beings, one is not called an Arhat.
Venerable Subhūti, this name 'Arhat' signifies that one does not sever the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, or the lineage of the Saṃgha."
In this way, the Arhat is able to sever all the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings;
in this way, the Arhat’s wisdom is inexhaustible, his merits are inexhaustible, and his eloquence is inexhaustible;
in this way, the Arhat is a companion to ordinary worldlings, not a companion to the noble ones.
"These are the World-Honored Ones worthy of offerings; those sentient beings who behold them attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.

At that time, there was a deva who constantly followed the Venerable Subhūti. Having not yet attained fixed determination, when he heard this discourse on the stage of being worthy of offerings, his heart was filled with joy, and he resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path to enlightenment.
Having thus resolved his mind, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"I now repent my transgressions; henceforth, I shall no longer follow the conduct of the Venerable One."
At that time, the son of good family asked the goddess,
"For what reason do you now repent before the Venerable Subhūti?
The goddess replied:

"For twelve years I have constantly followed the Venerable Subhūti, yet I never heard him speak of this stage of the Worthy One (Arhat). Now that I have heard of this stage of the Worthy One, I have resolved to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
I formed this thought:
"Wherever such teachings on the pure dharma of the worthy recipients are being proclaimed, I shall go there;
wherever an assembly of bodhisattvas gathers to expound the bodhisattva-dharma, I shall go to that place."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, hearing this goddess give rise to such a thought, immediately exhorted her, saying: "Goddess!
You have gained a great benefit, for you have resolved upon the unsurpassed path of enlightenment regarding the profound Dharma of the Buddha."
"O Goddess!
I am now afflicted by distress and heat, for I am not a vessel for the Dharma of omniscience. What should I do?"
"O Goddess!
If I had not yet severed all outflows (āsrava) and attained liberation of mind, I too would have resolved to attain the unsurpassed path.
O Goddess!"

"You should always thus draw near to spiritual friends, respectfully praising and circumambulating them to the right; by honoring such great and virtuous beings, you will also be able to hear the Dharma never heard before, and having heard this Dharma, you shall not forget it."
The Venerable Subhūti said to the goddess:
"I now likewise repent before you; it was because I did not originally understand your intention that I exhorted you toward the Dharma of the Śrāvakas."
The goddess replied:
"I am saying to the Venerable Subhūti that for a single sentient being, one should not encourage them toward the Śrāvaka vehicle without examining their faculties."
Why is this? Venerable Subhūti!
Those who seek the path to bodhi do not aspire to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
"Venerable Subhūti!
Although one may be oppressed by hunger and thirst, one will never eat food mixed with poison.
In this same way, Venerable Subhūti!"
"One who seeks to be a bodhisattva vows not to hear of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
At that time, this good man said to the goddess:
"The unsurpassed right path is extremely difficult to accomplish; if one’s adornments are slight, it is difficult to attain perfect awakening."
The goddess replied, “Noble son!
Although the unsurpassed right path is difficult to accomplish, I practice in this way so as not to abandon my progress.”
This son of good family asked the goddess,
"How do you practice?
The goddess replied:

"To practice a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, for the sake of being able to bear the burden of all sentient beings, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, and to cause all sentient beings to understand suffering and pleasure."
"Good son! I practice in this way.
The good son said:
“O Goddess! Those who grasp at signs lack an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
those who are bound by the fetters of self cannot liberate all sentient beings.”
Those who rely on the aggregates (skandhas) cannot shoulder the burden for all sentient beings;
those who harbor conceptualizations regarding various roots of goodness cannot bring all sentient beings to maturity;
and those who possess the notion of self and the notion of others cannot comprehend the suffering and happiness of sentient beings.
At that time, the goddess, following his instructions, attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
Then, outside the middle gate, the goddess scattered various kinds of flowers as an offering to this son of good family.
At that time, this son of good family manifested his original female form and attire, and said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, wait a moment; I shall bring food."
At that time, the woman immediately entered her home, brought food of a hundred flavors, and said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti!..."

"You are neither free from desire nor not free from desire; you are neither free from hatred nor not free from hatred; you are neither free from delusion nor not free from delusion; you are neither free from the fetters and latent tendencies nor not free from the fetters and latent tendencies—accept this food."
"Venerable Subhūti!
You who do not know suffering, do not abandon its origin, do not realize its cessation, and do not cultivate the path—accept this food."
"Venerable Subhūti!

If you do not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, do not cultivate the four right efforts, do not cultivate the four bases of psychic power, do not cultivate the five faculties, do not cultivate the five powers, do not cultivate the seven factors of awakening, and do not cultivate the eightfold noble path, then accept this food."
"Venerable Subhūti!
Since you have not given rise to the view of a self as a body and have attained the mind of the single path,
receive this food."
“Venerable Subhūti! You have extinguished ignorance and realized liberation;

you have advanced beyond all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). You do not engage with consciousness (*vijñāna*), and thus there is no further arising. Having attained liberation, you do not increase name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); you have transcended the three realms. Your six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are non-bases; you know the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*) and do not undergo contact (*sparśa*). You cultivate the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*), for you do not perceive sensation (*vedanā*).”

He has realized the liberation of wishlessness because he is free from craving; he understands that the grasping at suchness is immovable; he knows non-arising, he knows that existence is not an accumulation, he knows that birth is non-birth, and he knows that old age and death have no departure. He knows that the twelve links of dependent origination are without arising and without sustenance; you, however, partake of this sustenance.
"Venerable Subhūti!
You do not see the Buddha, you do not hear the Dharma, and you do not draw near to the Saṅgha, yet you receive this food.
Venerable One!"
If one knows that the five heinous crimes are identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one may accept this food.
Venerable One!
It is not that one will die here and be reborn elsewhere; rather, one accepts this food [with such understanding].
"Venerable One!

If the equanimity of greed is equal to the equanimity of non-contention, if the equanimity of hatred is equal to the equanimity of non-contention, and if the equanimity of delusion is equal to the equanimity of non-contention, then accept this food."
"Venerable sir!
You have not transcended the stage of ordinary beings, nor have you attained the stage of the noble ones; yet you accept this food.
Venerable sir!"
You do not enter from light into light; you neither fall into birth and death nor enter into nirvana; you speak neither true words nor false words—accept this food.

"Venerable One! You have exhausted the exhaustible and do not discriminate within the inexhaustible; you are unmoved even regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Your thoughts have no basis and are free from contention; you encounter no obstacles among sentient beings, and your mind is unbound by any phenomena. Accept this food."
"Venerable sir!
You have not attained this Dharma for which you went forth; therefore, do not accept this food, Venerable sir!"
Your aspiration for renunciation was not an aspiration to enter nirvana; therefore, accept this food.
If the Venerable Subhūti is without contention, then hell is also without contention.
"Venerable Subhūti!
Do not accept this food as one who is worthy of offerings.
Venerable Subhūti!"

If anyone should conceive the notion that you are one worthy of offerings, that person slanders the Great Virtue Subhūti; for you are not one worthy of offerings, nor are you one who has completed the act of giving, nor do you abide as one worthy of offerings.
"Venerable One!
If you accomplish this dharma, you may accept this food.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, standing outside the middle gate, moved his body seven times and extended his right hand, saying to the woman:
"Sister! Please explain this Dharma well for me so that I may accomplish it.
Then the woman sighed and said:
“Excellent! Excellent,
Venerable Subhūti!”
He then gave him the food.
Having given the food, he spoke these words:
"Venerable Subhūti!

Thus, the Arhats receive offerings with equanimity, a state difficult to encounter in the world; yet if one grants this equanimity out of pride, they will fall into hell despite having received pure offerings.
At that time, the goddess asked the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti!
For what reason does this girl preach such a Dharma, and why do you not answer her?"
Subhūti said: "Celestial maiden,
what do you think?"
"Can a phantom person say that this is a cause or not a cause?
The goddess replied, "No!"
"Venerable Subhūti. Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! As you have said, all phenomena are like illusions; what words could I possibly offer in reply?
O Goddess!"
If all sentient beings speak words that are either false or true, they are equal to me.
Why is this? Because these various utterances are spoken as being equal to an illusion.
While this method of receiving food was being practiced in such a manner, one hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the woman apologized to Subhūti; having apologized, she said to the Venerable Subhūti, “Please go as you please.
You take this food and go to where the Buddha is; I, too, shall go to where the Buddha is.”

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, carrying the alms he had collected, was leaving the city of Rājagṛha; because he had heard this Dharma, his heart was filled with joy and he found no pleasure in the food.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti thought to himself:
"To whom should I give this food? To whomsoever I give it, may the fruit of the gift not be lost.

Then there was a bodhisattva named Sarvadharmānavilekita (Unstained by All Dharmas), who, knowing what the Venerable Subhūti was thinking in his mind, went immediately to where the Venerable Subhūti was.
Having arrived, he said to the Venerable Subhūti,
"If you offer this food to me, its karmic fruit will not be lost.
Subhūti replied:
“Good son! Do you abide securely in the precepts?
He replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Within the non-appropriation of all phenomena, there is neither the observance of precepts nor their violation.
Venerable Subhūti!"
"I have committed killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti reflected upon what had been said:
"The eloquence attained by this son of good family is such that I shall now inquire about the causes and conditions for what he has spoken."
Subhūti said: "Good son!
For what reason do you speak these words?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Untainted by All Dharmas addressed the Venerable Subhūti in verse:
“My path is exceedingly pure, The unsurpassed path to bodhi.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings Dwell within this path.”
For this reason it is said: "I have slain all sentient beings"—this is called 'slaying sentient beings.
One who can purify this path does not receive enlightenment from the gods, nor does one receive it from Śakra or Brahmā.
"Without giving, one naturally attains [it]; for this reason, I have stolen it.
The Mahāyāna is without a giver; not relying on the Hīnayāna, I call this the Mahāyāna—for this reason, I have stolen it."
Knowing the nature of sexual misconduct, the wise seek the Dharma;
they do not pursue desire for the sake of desire, yet thus they practice such conduct.
According to whatever conventional designations exist, they speak them for those who thirst and yearn.
All false speech arises from this very cause.
If there are sentient beings who rely upon the Lesser Vehicle,
one should destroy such [attachments] and encourage them toward the Great Vehicle.
One who thus engages in divisive speech destroys the various non-Buddhists and causes sentient beings to fall into unwholesome paths;
yet such a person establishes others on level ground.
If one can censure [this behavior], there is no longer any talk of affectionate words.
He speaks harsh words to subdue all Māras;
he speaks harsh words yet his mind is free from anger.
The courageous one perceives skillful means for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Knowing what causes and conditions are being spoken of, yet speaking in accordance with those very causes and conditions—
this is called frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). Whether knowing the thoughts of billions of sentient beings,
or speaking of the truth, or knowing what constitutes falsehood;
For this reason, even through frivolous speech, one expounds the True Dharma.
If all sentient beings were to enjoy the pleasures of humans and devas,
yet further seek transcendence, one would hope for even a single such being.
If associated with joy and delight, it benefits those who tame the world;
the wise bestow upon all sentient beings happiness.
As for that which is taught regarding desire, that which is desired is likewise thus.
One should always make this vow: "May all sentient beings become Buddhas.
When the True Dharma is about to perish, may those who are courageous and steadfast uphold it;
even at the cost of their own bodies and lives, they shall not abandon the Buddha’s True Dharma."
Manifesting fearlessness toward all sentient beings who engage in disputes,
as well as all non-Buddhists, for the sake of upholding the True Dharma;
whether one were to encompass a single eon, or encompass ten million eons.
Because they do not abandon the True Dharma, they thereafter refrain from false speech.
The courageous one perceives that all conditioned phenomena are erroneous;
knowing them to be wrong views, he enters into Right View.
"One who possesses such a dharma as this abides securely in the upholding of the precepts;
one who dwells in non-dwelling—the wise one awakens to bodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti gave the alms he had received to the son of good family and spoke these words:
"This virtuous man should accept the offerings of the faithful without losing their karmic fruit.
On that day, the Venerable Subhūti did not eat; after the hour of *pūrva-āhna* had passed, he arose from samādhi and went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and related in full to the Buddha the teachings he had previously heard.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Do you now know the name of this bodhisattva?”
Subhūti said: “I do not know it,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva is named the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva ‘Transforming the Female Body,’ who teaches and transforms sentient beings through the skillful means of joyful adornment.”

Suppose, for example, in the kingdom of Magadha, ten *kharu* make one *khāri*, and one thousand *khāri* make one cartload. If there were as many mustard seeds as would fill one thousand such carts, someone might be able to count them to their very limit; yet they could not possibly count or know the number of sentient beings transformed by this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Turned-Woman (*Vivartitastri*) in the Sahā world through the skillful means of joyful adornment, causing all those humans and devas to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path to enlightenment.
At that time, this woman, surrounded and attended by five hundred women, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went toward Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw these women from afar and said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, do you see these five hundred women coming?"
Subhūti said, “I have seen them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"These women are all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have transformed their female bodies; they were brought to maturity through the skillful means of the Adornment of Joy, and have all already established themselves in the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment."

At that time, this woman, surrounded and attended by five hundred women, approached the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The five hundred women also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti went to where the woman was and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Have you now attained the dharmas of those who are not noble?"
"Do you now abide in the non-noble precepts?
Do you show reverence to women?
At that time, the woman said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Venerable sir!
Do you now know who in the world are noble and who are not?
If you cannot say, then you should remain silent.”
Śāriputra said: "Sister!
Are you able to discern between the noble and the non-noble?"
The woman said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I am able to know it."
Śāriputra said: "Sister!
How do you know this?"
The woman said:
"Venerable Sir!
If one does not sever the noble lineage, this is called 'noble'."
If one does not sever the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha, this is called being noble.
If one practices compassion with the desire to bring liberation to all who are not noble, this is called being noble.
"Venerable Śāriputra!

It would be better for a woman to adorn herself with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, wear garlands of *campaka* flowers, and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, yet never depart from the unsurpassed, right, and true mind of enlightenment and thus increase in holiness; this would be superior to an Arhat practicing the eight liberations and attaining the tranquility of the extinction of all outflows."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I shall now provide a simile: it is like placing a crystal bead in a lapis lazuli bowl, or setting a priceless jewel amidst filth and excrement.
Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
Śāriputra said, "Sister!"
"It would be better to place a priceless jewel in filth than to put a crystal bead in a lapis lazuli bowl.
"So it is, Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is a woman who dwells in the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true awakening, she surpasses all noble ones; she is superior to an Arhat who has cultivated the eight liberations, dwells in tranquility, and has severed all outflows."
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Sister, do you incline toward the Mahāyāna?"
The woman said:
"This essence of the Mahāyāna has neither departure nor return.
Śāriputra said:
“Sister!
If this Mahāyāna has neither departure nor return, where does the Mahāyāna tend?
The woman replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
This orientation toward the Great Vehicle is precisely the orientation toward the inexhaustibility of ignorance, and so on, up to the inexhaustibility of old age and death."
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!

Ignorance cannot be exhausted, and even old age and death cannot be exhausted. This inexhaustibility is precisely the dharma-nature of non-arising; if there were arising, there would be exhaustion, but since there is no arising, there is no exhaustion.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
A phenomenon produced through the conjunction of conditions is a phenomenon free from contention.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to select people?
World-Honored One!”
"And it is because this woman has adorned herself with these necklaces that she has attained such eloquence.
The woman said,
"Venerable Śāriputra!
"This eloquence is not an ornament for adornment.
Śāriputra said, "Sister!"
"Whose eloquence is this?
The woman replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!"

A Bodhisattva is adorned with eight kinds of necklaces; once adorned with them, they attain the unimpeded eloquence of a Bodhisattva. What are these eight? 1. The necklace-adornment of not losing the bodhicitta; 2. The necklace-adornment of abiding in the mind of ultimate great compassion; 3.

The necklace-adornment of having no obstructed mind toward any sentient being; 4. The necklace-adornment of seeking out extensive learning without ever becoming weary or satisfied; 5. The necklace-adornment of being well able to contemplate the teachings exactly as they have been heard; 6. The necklace-adornment of transforming all sentient beings while also not perceiving any phenomena; 7. The necklace-adornment of skillfully knowing the expedient means for discerning how profound dharmas arise through the conjunction of conditions; 8. The necklace-adornment of skillfully knowing the faculties of all sentient beings and being upheld by all Buddhas through skillful means.
Venerable Śāriputra!
These are called the eight kinds of necklaces and ornaments; if a bodhisattva adorns themselves with these necklaces and ornaments, they will attain unimpeded eloquence.
